tiers.name: Just you
tiers.blurb: Nobody depends on this yet. Start with what costs nothing: secure your account, keep secrets out of the repo, and give people a private way to report bugs.

tiers.name: First fans
tiers.blurb: Someone starred or installed it. Your CI and your releases are now someone else's supply chain.

tiers.name: Getting noticed
tiers.blurb: Strangers send PRs. Assume some of them are hostile and make CI safe to run on their code.

tiers.name: Small community
tiers.blurb: Other projects build on you. Write down how you handle a vulnerability before you need to.

tiers.name: Established
tiers.blurb: Attackers now find you worth targeting. Prove what you ship and make releases tamper-evident.

tiers.name: Widely used
tiers.blurb: A bug here becomes a CVE downstream. Fuzz continuously and rehearse your incident plan.

tiers.name: Load-bearing
tiers.blurb: Other people's systems depend on your code. Get an outside audit and make your builds reproducible.

tiers.name: Critical infrastructure
tiers.blurb: The ecosystem's security depends on yours. Do everything, and help your dependencies do it too.

tier_note: A repo's tier is the higher of its stars tier and its dependents tier (dependents = repositories + packages on GitHub's dependency graph). Thresholds are a starting point: dependents carry more weight than stars because they measure real blast radius.

layers.label: Public scan
layers.blurb: Anyone can run it. Reads files, workflows and public settings. Nothing to install.

layers.label: Private scan (download)
layers.blurb: Run sosf-scan.mjs on your machine with your own token. Sees admin-only settings. The report never leaves your browser.

layers.label: GitHub App
layers.blurb: Install the app on a repo to check admin settings from the site and apply safe fixes with one click.

layers.label: Self-check
layers.blurb: Things a scan can only sometimes settle, such as training, audits and process. Tick them off when they're done.

attacks.title: A maintainer account is taken over
attacks.story: A phished password or stolen session lets an attacker push code, merge PRs or publish a release as you.

attacks.title: A pull request attacks your CI
attacks.story: A stranger opens a PR whose title, branch name or code runs inside a privileged workflow and steals your token or secrets.

attacks.title: A dependency or action is compromised
attacks.story: A popular action or package you use is hijacked (tj-actions, Shai-Hulud) and runs attacker code in your builds.

attacks.title: A release is tampered with
attacks.story: An attacker publishes a malicious version under your name, or swaps an artifact after release.

attacks.title: A secret leaks
attacks.story: A token lands in a commit, a log or a workflow artifact and someone uses it before you notice.

attacks.title: A bug in your code is exploited
attacks.story: Untrusted input reaches a parser or query and crashes it, corrupts data or runs attacker code.

attacks.title: A vulnerability report goes badly
attacks.story: A researcher can't reach you privately, files a public issue, and users are exposed before a fix exists.

attacks.title: AI features or AI contributions are abused
attacks.story: Prompt injection makes an agent leak data or run tools; low-quality AI reports and PRs bury real ones.

attacks.title: Someone you trust goes rogue
attacks.story: A long-time contributor or a social-engineered co-maintainer slips in a backdoor (the xz pattern).

items.label: Require 2FA for everyone in the org
items.title: Require two-factor authentication
items.short: Turn on 2FA for yourself and require it for everyone with write access.
items.why: A phished or reused password is the cheapest way into a project: it lets an attacker push code or cut a release as you. Requiring 2FA for everyone with write access means a leaked password alone doesn't get anyone in.
steps: Turn on 2FA for your own account: Settings → Password and authentication → Enable two-factor authentication. Use an authenticator app rather than SMS, and save the recovery codes offline.
In an org, first list who lacks 2FA (snippet below) and warn them: members lose access to org resources until they enable it, and outside collaborators are removed.
Then open the org's Settings → Authentication security, tick "Require two-factor authentication for everyone in your organization", and save.
To shut out SMS as well, also tick "Only allow secure two-factor methods"; FS2 now requires secure methods across the Typelevel org.
On a personal account you can't enforce 2FA for collaborators. Ask each one to confirm they use it, or move the project into an organization.

snippets.label: Who would be locked out or removed? (run as an org owner before enforcing)
snippets.code:
# Members and outside collaborators with no 2FA at all
gh api "orgs/{owner}/members?filter=2fa_disabled" --paginate --jq '.[].login'
gh api "orgs/{owner}/outside_collaborators?filter=2fa_disabled" --paginate --jq '.[].login'

# Before ticking "Only allow secure two-factor methods": who still has SMS or another insecure method?
gh api "orgs/{owner}/members?filter=2fa_insecure" --paginate --jq '.[].login'

pitfalls: Bot and service accounts added as outside collaborators are removed too, unless you set up 2FA on them first.
Losing your phone without recovery codes can lock you out of your own project. Keep the codes in a password manager or on paper.

items.label: Use passkeys or hardware keys (not SMS/TOTP)
items.title: Use passkeys or hardware keys
items.short: Sign in with a passkey or security key so a fake login page can't steal your 2FA.
items.why: App codes and SMS codes can be typed into a look-alike site. In September 2025 the maintainer of chalk and debug entered his password and 2FA code on a fake npm page, and malware shipped in 18 packages with billions of weekly downloads within hours. A passkey only works on the real domain, so that phish fails.
steps: On GitHub, go to Settings → Password and authentication → Passkeys → Add a passkey. If a hardware security key is already registered, choose "Upgrade to passkey" instead.
Use an authenticator app, not SMS, as your base 2FA method; GitHub requires an app or SMS before you can register security keys.
Register two authenticators, such as a phone passkey and a hardware key, and keep your recovery codes, so one lost device doesn't lock you out.
Do the same on your package registries: npm and PyPI both accept WebAuthn security keys, and PyPI prefers them because they resist phishing.
If you run an org, tick "Only allow secure two-factor methods" under Authentication security to block accounts that still have SMS configured.
pitfalls: Your password plus app code still works as a fallback, so the passkey only protects you if you use it. If a login page asks for a 6-digit code when you expected a passkey prompt, stop and check the address.
A passkey that lives on a single phone disappears with it. Use a synced passkey or register a second key.

items.label: Least-privilege roles; prune admins, stale members and outside collaborators
items.title: Give the fewest people the fewest rights
items.short: Give each person the lowest role that fits their work and remove access nobody uses.
items.why: Every admin, write collaborator, deploy key and app is another way to push code as the project. Nasiko audited who had access to what and removed unnecessary permissions so "a single compromised account reaches less"; Fastify wrote scripts that offboard members to an emeritus team and flag inactive accounts.
steps: List who has access: Settings → Collaborators & teams for each repo, and the People page for an org (snippet below).
Downgrade roles: Triage for people who label and close issues, Write for people who merge, Admin for one or two owners. Set the org base permission to Read or No permission.
Remove people inactive for a year or more, or move them to an emeritus team as Fastify does. Ask them first whether their account is still safe.
Review deploy keys, webhooks and installed GitHub Apps, and delete what you don't recognize. A deploy key keeps working even after the person who added it leaves the org.
Do the same cleanup on your package registry; Fastify syncs its npm teams with its GitHub repo topics and removes npm access when someone leaves.
In an org, invite regular maintainers as members rather than outside collaborators, as FS2 did, so you can manage their access through teams.

snippets.label: Who can push or administer? (run with admin rights)
snippets.code:
gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/collaborators --paginate --jq '.[] | "\(.role_name)\t\(.login)"'
gh api "orgs/{owner}/members?role=admin" --paginate --jq '.[].login'   # org owners
gh api orgs/{owner}/outside_collaborators --paginate --jq '.[].login'
gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/keys --jq '.[] | "\(.read_only)\t\(.title)\t\(.created_at)"'   # deploy keys

pitfalls: Org owners always have admin access to every repo in the org, so keep the owner list short.
Don't put an admin token in CI to automate membership. Fastify runs its org-admin scripts locally, with --dryRun, so a compromised workflow can't rewrite who has access.

items.label: Secure package-registry accounts (2FA, scoped or no long-lived tokens)
items.title: Lock down your package registry accounts
items.short: Protect npm, PyPI and other registry accounts with strong 2FA and few owners.
items.why: Whoever controls your registry account can publish a malicious version under your name without touching your repo. The Shai-Hulud worm (September 2025) ran in npm install scripts, took the publish tokens it found and pushed infected versions of more packages. Fastify turned "who can publish fastify?" into a question with a reproducible answer by scripting its npm team membership and keeping publish tokens out of CI.
steps: Turn on 2FA with a security key or passkey on every registry account that can publish (PyPI requires 2FA; npm supports WebAuthn keys), and store recovery codes offline.
On npm, if you publish by hand, set each package's Settings → Publishing access to "Require two-factor authentication and disallow tokens".
Publish from CI with trusted publishing instead of stored tokens. npm will stop direct publishing with granular tokens in January 2027.
List everyone who can publish (npm owners and org teams, PyPI collaborators) and remove people who no longer maintain the package.
Revoke tokens you can't account for. If you must keep one, scope it to a single package and give it an expiry date.
Turn on 2FA for the email account behind each registry login, since password resets go there.

snippets.label: npm: who can publish, and which tokens exist on your account
snippets.code:
npm owner ls <package>
npm access list collaborators <package>
npm token list
npm token revoke <id>   # anything you can't account for

pitfalls: Logging in to npm with a recovery code puts a 72-hour hold on the account: no publishing and no new tokens. Don't burn one in the middle of a release.
One token that can publish every package is a single point of failure.

items.label: Protect the default branch (rulesets: reviews, status checks, no force-push)
items.title: Protect your default branch
items.short: Block force pushes and direct pushes to your default branch with a ruleset.
items.why: Without it, a stolen token or a tired maintainer can push straight to main or rewrite its history, and CI never gets a say. GitHub Security Lab calls it the setting with the biggest impact because it makes code scanning and Dependabot findings block merges.
steps: Go to Settings → Rulesets → New ruleset → New branch ruleset, set enforcement to Active, and add the default branch as the target.
Keep "Restrict deletions" and "Block force pushes" on, and turn on "Require a pull request before merging".
With two or more maintainers, require one approval. Solo, set approvals to 0 so PRs still run CI, or give the Repository admin role a "For pull requests only" bypass.
Once CI is stable, add "Require status checks to pass before merging" with your test and CodeQL checks.
Prefer rulesets to classic protection: anyone with read access can see them, and Scorecard can check them without an admin token.
After migrating, delete the old classic rule. Both apply at once and the stricter one wins, which confuses people.

pitfalls: Requiring an approval when you're the only maintainer blocks your own PRs; oapi-codegen's solo maintainer had no second reviewer for his own changes.
An "Always allow" bypass for admins means a stolen admin token is as powerful as before. Keep the bypass list short.

items.label: Protect tags and use immutable releases
items.title: Make releases immutable and protect tags
items.short: Turn on immutable releases and protect version tags with a tag ruleset.
items.why: Without these, anyone who takes over a maintainer account or a write token can move a release tag to new code or swap a binary in an old release, and users pinned to that version get the attacker's build.
steps: In Settings → General → Releases, tick "Enable release immutability". It applies only to releases published from then on.
Change your release process to: create a draft, attach every asset (binaries, checksums, SBOM, signatures), then publish.
In Settings → Rules → Rulesets, choose New tag ruleset, target v* (or all tags), and add Restrict creations, Restrict updates, Restrict deletions and Block force pushes.
Set the ruleset's enforcement status to Active; a new ruleset starts out disabled.
Put only release maintainers, or the GitHub App your release workflow uses, on the bypass list.
Point users to gh release verify and gh release verify-asset to check a release and its files against the release attestation.

snippets.label: Draft, attach, then publish (the release locks on publish)
snippets.code:
gh release create v1.2.3 --draft --verify-tag --title "v1.2.3" --notes-file CHANGES.md
gh release upload v1.2.3 dist/* sbom.spdx.json
gh release edit v1.2.3 --draft=false

# Anyone can then check the release and a downloaded file
gh release verify v1.2.3
gh release verify-asset v1.2.3 ./mytool-1.2.3.tar.gz

pitfalls: Once an immutable release is published you can't add, replace or delete its assets, so a workflow that uploads after publishing (for example on release: published) will fail.
Deleting an immutable release doesn't free its tag name; you can't reuse it.
Restrict creations applies to workflows too. If CI pushes your tags, give that actor bypass (a GitHub App works) or create tags by hand.

items.label: CODEOWNERS, especially for workflows and release config
items.title: Require owner review for workflows and release config
items.short: Make a maintainer's review mandatory for changes to workflows and release config.
items.why: A PR that edits .github/workflows/ or your release scripts can change what runs with your secrets on the next push, and in a busy queue it can look like a routine fix. CODEOWNERS plus required code owner review makes sure someone who understands CI signs off.
steps: Create .github/CODEOWNERS covering /.github/, release and packaging config, and SECURITY.md. GitHub uses the copy on the PR's base branch, so a PR can't change who reviews it.
In your default-branch ruleset, edit "Require a pull request before merging" and require review from Code Owners. One owner's approval is enough.
Owners need write access, and teams must be visible with write permission, or GitHub assigns no owner. Open the file on GitHub to see any errors.
Order matters: the last matching pattern wins, so put broad rules first and specific paths after.
Update the file when people leave.

snippets.label: CODEOWNERS covering CI and release config (adjust paths to your stack)

pitfalls: CODEOWNERS on its own only requests reviews. Without the ruleset option, PRs still merge without an owner's approval.
In an org, write teams as @org/team-name; a bare @org is not a valid owner.
With a single owner, required owner review blocks your own PRs. Turn it on once two people can approve.

items.label: Require signed commits
items.title: Require signed commits
items.short: Sign your commits and require verified signatures on the default branch.
items.why: Git lets anyone write any name and email into a commit, so an unsigned commit that claims to be from you proves nothing. Requiring signatures ties every commit on main to a key its author controls. Electron, Next.js, Turborepo and shadcn/ui enforce it with a ruleset.
steps: Each maintainer sets up signing. SSH signing reuses a key you already have and needs Git 2.34 or later (snippet below).
Add the public key under Settings → SSH and GPG keys → New SSH key, choosing the signing key type. A login key must be uploaded again for signing.
Turn on vigilant mode so unsigned commits that claim to be yours show as Unverified.
Explain the requirement in CONTRIBUTING.md first, then add "Require signed commits" to your default-branch ruleset.
Merge with squash or merge commits. GitHub can't sign commits it rebases, so "Rebase and merge" doesn't fit a branch that requires signatures.

snippets.label: Sign commits and tags with your SSH key
snippets.code:
git config --global gpg.format ssh
git config --global user.signingkey ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
git config --global commit.gpgsign true
git config --global tag.gpgSign true

# Upload the same public key as a signing key (separate from its login entry)
gh ssh-key add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub --type signing --title "commit signing"

pitfalls: Unsigned commits in a contributor's PR can block even a squash merge. They have to re-sign them, or someone with bypass rights merges.
Signing won't stop someone using your logged-in browser: GitHub signs commits made in its web UI with its own key.

items.label: Apply an org-wide security configuration across repos
items.title: Apply one security configuration to every repo
items.short: Create one org security configuration and apply it to every repo, including new ones.
items.why: Per-repo toggles drift: new repos start with features off, and nobody notices which of 40 packages lacks push protection. FS2 built a configuration with private vulnerability reporting and applied it to all of Typelevel's public repos, and Yii found configurations "Very useful for Yii3, which has many packages."
steps: Go to the org's Settings → Advanced Security → Configurations → New configuration → Custom configuration.
Turn on what's free for public repos: secret scanning and push protection, dependency graph, Dependabot alerts and security updates, code scanning default setup, and private vulnerability reporting.
For code scanning, choose "Enabled with advanced setup allowed", which only turns on default setup where CodeQL isn't already running.
Under Policy, set "Use as default for newly created repositories" to Public or All, and choose Enforce if repo admins shouldn't switch features off.
On the Repositories tab, select all and use Apply configuration. Check each repo's status, and apply it by hand to repos transferred in later.
Personal accounts have no configurations; loop over your repos with gh api instead.

snippets.label: Apply an existing configuration to all public repos and make it the default
snippets.code:
gh api orgs/{owner}/code-security/configurations --jq '.[] | "\(.id)\t\(.name)"'
gh api -X POST orgs/{owner}/code-security/configurations/<id>/attach -f scope=public
gh api -X PUT orgs/{owner}/code-security/configurations/<id>/defaults -f default_for_new_repos=public

pitfalls: Secret Protection and Code Security cost money on private and internal repos. Scope the configuration to public repos unless you have licenses.
A configuration doesn't cover org-wide settings such as required 2FA; set those separately.

items.label: Review repository and org security settings regularly
items.title: Review your settings on a schedule
items.short: Put a recurring date on the calendar to re-check access, apps, keys and settings.
items.why: Settings drift: a collaborator from three years ago keeps write access, a webhook still posts to a service you stopped using, a feature gets switched off while debugging. ImageMagick's advice after the program was to "Regularly review GitHub's security best practices and updates", and actix-web's settings review is what led it to require 2FA.
steps: Every 3 to 6 months, and whenever a maintainer leaves, run the snippet below or walk the same list in Settings.
Access: remove stale collaborators, outside collaborators and org owners; check deploy keys, webhooks and installed GitHub Apps.
Security features: secret scanning, push protection, private vulnerability reporting and Dependabot still on, and rulesets active with a short bypass list.
Actions: the default token still read-only, approval still required for first-time contributors' workflows, and no unused repository secrets.
Accounts: read your own security log, which covers the last 90 days, and for an org the audit log, looking for changes you didn't make.
Close gaps with GitHub Security Lab's "Protect Your Project" guided flow, which covers six core settings in under half an hour, or with OpenSSF Scorecard.

snippets.label: Quick settings review for one repo (run as a repo admin)
snippets.code:
R={owner}/{repo}
gh api repos/$R --jq '.security_and_analysis'
gh api repos/$R/private-vulnerability-reporting
gh api repos/$R/actions/permissions/workflow
gh api repos/$R/rulesets --jq '.[] | {name, target, enforcement}'
gh api repos/$R/collaborators --paginate --jq '.[] | "\(.role_name)\t\(.login)"'
gh api repos/$R/keys --jq '.[] | {title, read_only, created_at}'
gh api repos/$R/hooks --jq '.[] | {url: .config.url, active}'
gh api repos/$R/actions/secrets --jq '.secrets[] | {name, updated_at}'

pitfalls: Some settings, such as security_and_analysis, are only visible to admins. Run the review with admin rights or everything will look switched off.
A setting that's wrong in one repo is usually wrong in all of them. Fix it everywhere, or with an org configuration.

items.label: Publish SECURITY.md (how to report, supported versions, response times)
items.title: Publish a SECURITY.md
items.short: Publish a SECURITY.md that says how to report privately and what happens next.
items.why: Without one, a well-meaning reporter's options are a public issue, which is now a public exploit, or your personal email if they can find it. A policy can also say what not to report; SciPy's does, to cut false reports.
steps: Start from the template and put the file in .github/, the repo root, or docs/.
Give a private channel: the private vulnerability reporting link plus an email fallback. virtualenv and n8n-MCP both added a contact email to theirs.
Say which versions get fixes, what's in scope and what isn't, and what helps a report: version, reproduction, impact.
Set response targets you can keep. actix-web calls its times "targets rather than a strict SLA" because volunteers maintain it; DocsGPT promises acknowledgment within 48 hours.
Maintaining several repos? Put one SECURITY.md in your public .github repository; every repo without its own shows it (snippet below).
Link it from your README and docs, and re-read it when maintainers or supported versions change.

snippets.label: Share one policy across every repo you own (run outside your project folder)
snippets.code:
gh repo create {owner}/.github --public --clone   # or: gh repo clone {owner}/.github
cp /path/to/SECURITY.md .github/SECURITY.md
cd .github
git add SECURITY.md && git commit -m "Add default security policy"
git push -u origin HEAD

pitfalls: An inbox nobody reads. Test the address, and make sure at least two people receive it.
Asking reporters to open an issue with a security label: issues are public.
Promising a 24/7 response you can't give. GitHub Security Lab points to systemd's policy as an example that sets expectations without one.

Please do not open a public issue. Report it privately through GitHub:

items.label: Enable private vulnerability reporting
items.title: Turn on private vulnerability reporting
items.short: Turn on private vulnerability reporting so researchers never need a public issue.
items.why: A vulnerability filed as a public issue is disclosed before a fix exists and "starts a clock you did not choose", as Nasiko put it. With private reporting on, reports arrive on your Advisories page, where you can accept one as a draft advisory, fix it in a temporary private fork and publish when ready.
steps: Settings → Advanced Security → click Enable next to "Private vulnerability reporting" (public repos).
Make sure you'll see reports: GitHub only notifies admins and security managers who watch the repo, so set Watch → Custom → Security alerts and allow email.
Point SECURITY.md at the "Report a vulnerability" form so reporters don't fall back to issues.
Triage each report: accept it as a draft, ask questions in comments, or close it with a short explanation. Use confidential comments to talk among maintainers.
Optionally add .github/VULNERABILITY_REPORT.yml to require details such as a proof of concept, and set rate limits to curb spam.
For many repos, enable it through an org security configuration, as FS2 did for every public repo, or with the loop below.

snippets.label: Turn it on for every public repo you own
snippets.code:
gh repo list {owner} --visibility public --no-archived --source --limit 1000 \
  --json nameWithOwner --jq '.[].nameWithOwner' |
while read -r r; do
  gh api -X PUT "repos/$r/private-vulnerability-reporting" --silent && echo "on: $r"
done

pitfalls: Turning it on without watching the repo: reports can sit unseen for weeks.
Leaving an old SECURITY.md that tells people to open an issue, or to email someone who has left.

items.label: Set triage and response time targets
items.title: Set response times for reports
items.short: Publish realistic response targets and a clear scope for vulnerability reports.
items.why: Reporters go public when they hear nothing, and maintainers burn out on out-of-scope reports. Teams set targets they could keep: DocsGPT acknowledges within 48 hours, and actix-web treats its times as targets because volunteers run it. Some also narrowed their scope: Vapor stopped issuing advisories for its dependencies' vulnerabilities, and Yii may rule a report out of scope when it depends on ignoring several documented practices.
steps: Pick targets you can meet in a bad month, such as acknowledging in 3 business days and assessing in 10; the OpenSSF guide suggests acknowledging within 1 to 2 days.
Stay inside the Best Practices badge bar: a first response within 14 days, and no medium or higher issue left unpatched 60 days after it becomes public.
Write down what's out of scope (snippet below) and link it when closing reports. aiohttp's threat model lets AI-assisted reporters check scope before filing.
Agree the disclosure date with each reporter. 90 days is the longest common default, and many are shorter.
Name who triages and who backs them up; CocoIndex wrote down who gets involved, how they communicate and how quickly fixes ship.
Send short status updates while you work. Silence is what pushes reporters to disclose early.

snippets.label: "What to expect" and "Out of scope" sections for SECURITY.md
snippets.code:
## What to expect

We are volunteers, so these are targets, not guarantees.

| Step | Target |
| --- | --- |
| Acknowledge your report | 3 business days |
| First assessment (valid? severity?) | 10 business days |
| Status updates while we work | every 2 weeks |
| Fix and disclosure date | agreed with you, usually within 90 days |

## Out of scope

- Vulnerabilities in our dependencies that our code doesn't expose: please report them upstream.
- Problems that only occur when the security guidance in our docs is ignored.
- Reports without a reproduction or a concrete impact.
- Missing hardening that doesn't lead to an exploit.

pitfalls: Promising an SLA you can't keep. One missed deadline costs more trust than a modest target.
Waving off every dependency CVE. If you ship or pin the vulnerable code, it's your issue too.

items.label: Publish GitHub security advisories and request CVEs (GitHub is a CNA)
items.title: Publish advisories and get CVEs
items.short: Publish a GitHub security advisory for every fixed vulnerability and request a CVE.
items.why: A silent fix leaves downstream users exposed, because Dependabot, audit tools and scanners only flag vulnerable versions once an advisory exists. GitHub is a CVE Numbering Authority and usually reviews CVE requests within 72 hours.
steps: Open the Security tab → Advisories → New draft security advisory, or accept a private report as a draft.
Fill in affected and patched versions, severity (the CVSS calculator helps) and CWE, and credit the reporter unless they decline.
Fix it in a temporary private fork, so the patch isn't public before the release.
Click "Request CVE" at the bottom of the advisory. It stays private while GitHub reviews it; public repos only.
Release the fix, then publish the advisory and flag it in the release notes. GitHub reviews it for the Advisory Database, which drives Dependabot alerts in affected repos.
If another CNA covers your project, such as your foundation, request the CVE there; GitHub can't assign one.

snippets.label: Advisory description outline
snippets.code:
### Impact
What kind of vulnerability this is, who is affected, and under which configuration.

### Patches
Fixed in <version>. Users of <affected range> should upgrade.

### Workarounds
A configuration change users can make until they upgrade, or "None".

### References
- Fix: https://github.com/{owner}/{repo}/commit/<sha>
- Release notes: https://github.com/{owner}/{repo}/releases/tag/<version>

pitfalls: Publishing without a patched version: Dependabot then alerts every user with no safe version to move to.
Fixing in a public PR titled "fix XSS" before the release tells attackers where to look.
Temporary private forks don't run CI, so test the fix locally before merging.

items.label: Coordinate disclosure with downstream/upstream and notify providers or registries
items.title: Coordinate fixes with downstream users
items.short: Agree a disclosure date with the reporter and give key downstream users time to patch.
items.why: Some fixes need other people: a distribution, a hosted service or an upstream library. aiohttp's decompression-bomb fix (CVE-2025-69223) had to wait for Google to ship brotli 1.2, and Node.js ships coordinated security releases across its supported lines.
steps: Agree a public date with the reporter early. 90 days is the longest common default; release Monday to Wednesday and avoid holidays.
If an upstream library needs the fix, report it privately upstream and add its maintainers as collaborators on your draft advisory.
Decide whether anyone needs advance notice. The OpenSSF guide says that mostly applies to projects with a large vendor or hosted-service ecosystem.
If so, send an embargoed notice 1 to 30 working days before release with the CVE, summary, affected versions, fix and public date (template below).
Keep a private list of downstream contacts in your incident plan; OpenClaw has a direct vulnerability-sync line with Tencent's security team.
On release day, publish the advisory, label the release notes as a security fix, and credit the reporter.

snippets.label: Embargoed pre-notification
snippets.code:
Subject: [EMBARGOED until <date> <time> UTC] {repo} security release

This is a private notice. Do not share it or ship the fix before the date above.

Issue:       CVE-XXXX-NNNNN (GHSA-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx), severity <level>
Summary:     One or two sentences on the flaw and its impact.
Affected:    {repo} <first affected> to <last affected>
Fixed in:    <version>, published at the time above
Mitigation:  Workaround until you can upgrade, if any.
Credit:      <reporter, as they prefer>
Contact:     <security contact from SECURITY.md>

Please reply to confirm you received this, and tell us at once if it looks like it has leaked.

pitfalls: Pre-notifying a long list: every extra reader raises the chance of a leak.
Letting the agreed date slip without telling the reporter. Ask for more time early, and explain why.

items.label: Write (and publish) a threat model
items.title: Write a threat model
items.short: Write down what you protect, where untrusted input enters, and what could go wrong.
items.why: Without a map, reviews and scanners spend their time in the wrong places, and every report turns into an argument about intended behavior. aiohttp's STRIDE model covers nineteen subsystems from the HTTP parser to the release pipeline and lets AI-assisted reporters check scope, and DocsGPT found its public model doubles as "a map for automated reviewers".
steps: Start small with your most exposed part, such as a parser, authentication or the release pipeline. Sniffnet ranked its assets by likelihood and impact first.
List assets and entry points. Readest asks: what user data does this touch, which input can someone else control, what crosses into native code, who can publish?
At each trust boundary, walk STRIDE (spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, elevation of privilege) and note mitigations and gaps.
Include the path to users: GitHub Actions, tags, releases and registry credentials, as actix-web's model does.
Mark what is the user's responsibility, publish the model and link it from SECURITY.md. Keep unfixed gaps private; ImageMagick kept its whole model private.
Revisit it when you add an input format or feature, and feed each new advisory back in, as aiohttp now does.

snippets.label: Threat-model questions for feature PRs (adapted from Readest)
snippets.code:
### Security questions (new features)
- What user data does this touch?
- Which input can someone outside the project control?
- Does anything cross into native code, a shell, or a network call?
- Does this change who or what can publish a release?
- Does THREAT_MODEL.md need an update?

pitfalls: Trying to cover everything at once. Termux put its model off because the full scope would take weeks.
Writing it once. A model that predates your last three features misleads more than it helps.

new_file.template:
# Threat model

Last reviewed: YYYY-MM-DD

## What we protect (assets)
- Users' data processed by the library
- The release pipeline and published packages
- Maintainer accounts and CI secrets

## Trust boundaries
- Untrusted input: files, network data, user-supplied strings
- Untrusted contributors: pull requests and issues
- Third parties: dependencies, GitHub Actions, registries

## Threats (STRIDE)
| Threat | Where | Mitigation | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Spoofing a maintainer | GitHub, registry | 2FA with passkeys, trusted publishing | |
| Tampering with releases | CI, registry | immutable releases, provenance | |
| Info disclosure of secrets | CI logs | least-privilege tokens, OIDC | |
| Denial of service | parser | input limits, fuzzing | |
| Elevation via CI | workflows | no pull_request_target with PR code | |

## Out of scope
- Applications that pass untrusted input to APIs documented as unsafe

## Review triggers
Revisit this when you add a new input format, a new release channel or an AI feature.

items.short: Write a short incident plan: who leads, and how you triage, fix, disclose and recover.
items.why: "A plan written during a crisis inherits the crisis," as Nasiko put it: severity, disclosure and who to call get decided at the worst possible moment. aiohttp's plan, for example, covers severity tiers, an advisory-to-release runbook, and playbooks for a compromised release pipeline, maintainer account or CI.
steps: Start from the template. Name an incident lead and a backup, and how to reach them outside GitHub.
Define severity levels and what each one triggers. actix-web separates code vulnerabilities, release integrity issues, security regressions and dependency issues.
Write the vulnerability path: acknowledge, open a draft advisory, fix in a private fork, request a CVE, release, publish, notify.
Add playbooks for incidents that aren't bug reports: a compromised account, a leaked token, a malicious release on the registry, a hijacked workflow.
List contacts (GitHub Support, your registry's security team, key downstream projects) and check them whenever maintainers change.
Publish a short public version and keep sensitive details internal, as Mockoon did. ImageMagick drew its process as a Mermaid diagram in SECURITY.md (snippet below).

snippets.label: Process diagram for SECURITY.md (GitHub renders Mermaid blocks)
snippets.code:
flowchart TD

pitfalls: Planning only for vulnerability reports. Account and pipeline compromises need different first steps, like revoking tokens and yanking releases.
A plan nobody has practiced. Run a one-hour drill once a year.

new_file.template:
# Incident response plan

## Roles
- Incident lead: {person}
- Backup: (name a second maintainer)

## Severity
- Critical: active exploitation, compromised release or account
- High: exploitable vulnerability, no known exploitation
- Medium/Low: hard to exploit or limited impact

## Steps
1. Acknowledge the report (target: 3 business days) and open a private advisory.
2. Contain: revoke tokens, yank or deprecate bad releases, lock down the repo if an account is compromised.
3. Fix in the private advisory fork; request a CVE.
4. Release the fix, publish the advisory, notify downstream projects and registries.
5. Write a short post-incident review within two weeks.

## Contacts
- GitHub Security: https://github.com/contact
- Package registry security team: (add yours)
- Downstream projects to notify: (list them)

items.label: Rehearse the incident response plan and review past incidents
items.title: Rehearse the plan and learn from past incidents
items.short: Run a one-hour drill of your incident plan every year, using a fake report.
items.why: The first real run of a plan always finds gaps: a contact who left, missing registry rights, nobody who has requested a CVE before. FS2 reviewed past Typelevel incidents to bring new Security Team members up to speed.
steps: Book an hour with everyone named in the plan, once a year and whenever a maintainer joins.
Pick a scenario: a fake private report, a leaked publish token, or a malicious release on your registry.
Use the real tools: open a draft advisory titled DRILL, start a temporary private fork, rate severity and draft the text, then close the draft.
Time each step and note blockers: missing permissions, stale contacts, steps nobody understood.
Also replay a past incident, yours or a public one like the tj-actions compromise, and ask what your plan would have done.
Update the plan the same day and record the drill date in it.

snippets.label: Drill card
snippets.code:
## Drill: leaked publish token (60 minutes)

Scenario: "The publish token for {repo} appeared in a public CI log two hours ago."

1. Who leads, and who is backup? Can both be reached right now?
2. Revoke the token. Who has the rights, and how long did it take?
3. Check the registry's release history. Any versions you didn't publish?
4. Decide: yank or deprecate? Advisory? Who tells users, and where?
5. Practice the advisory in a draft titled DRILL, then close it.

Record blockers, missing access and outdated contacts. Fix the plan today.

pitfalls: Requesting a CVE or publishing during a drill. Never press those buttons on a practice advisory.
Drilling only the person who wrote the plan. The backup needs the practice most.

items.label: Get an independent security audit or expert review
items.title: Get an independent audit or expert review
items.short: Have outside experts review your riskiest code once the basics are in place.
items.why: Maintainers can't easily see their own blind spots. aiohttp's audit by Radically Open Security, arranged through NLnet's NGI Zero program, led to five CVEs, and a later Trail of Bits review found 10 more issues (8 CVEs). Gleam's review with GitHub Security Lab and the EEF security team found no gaps, which still mattered: "Being secure is one thing; having confidence in security is another."
steps: Do the basics in this checklist first, so auditors spend their time on design and code. OSTIF asks projects to run its preliminary checks before an audit.
Scope it to the riskiest parts, such as parsers, authentication, crypto, sandboxing or the release pipeline, and hand over your threat model and build instructions.
Find funding: NGI Zero grantees can request an audit by Radically Open Security, and OSTIF scopes audits, picks auditors and helps raise the money; initial audits run from about $30k to $200k.
Reserve maintainer time to fix the findings; NLnet also paid for the time aiohttp spent fixing.
Handle findings like any report, with private advisories, CVEs and a coordinated release; aiohttp shipped eight advisories together in 3.13.3.
Publish the report once fixes ship, and repeat after big changes. Stalwart's second audit came two years after its first.
pitfalls: Treating a clean audit as permanent. New features need fresh eyes.
Booking an audit with no time set aside to fix what it finds.

items.label: Publish a post-mortem after an incident
items.title: Publish a post-mortem after incidents
items.short: After an incident, publish what happened, who was affected and what you changed.
items.why: Users need to know whether they were affected and what to do, and a clear account rebuilds trust faster than silence. After the March 2025 breach of its test infrastructure, Node.js published a full disclosure with a timeline, remediation and long-term prevention; PyPI's analysis of the Ultralytics attack showed that the later malicious uploads, which had no attestations, came through an old API token.
steps: Within two weeks of containment, write it up (template below): summary, impact, timeline in UTC, root cause, fixes and what users should do.
Keep it blameless: describe decisions and systems, not people.
Name the exact affected versions, artifacts and time window, so users can check their lockfiles and logs.
Publish where users look: a GitHub advisory if it's a vulnerability, the release notes, and your blog or discussions. Link it from SECURITY.md.
Turn follow-ups into backlog items, and update your threat model and incident plan.

items.label: Least-privilege GITHUB_TOKEN (explicit, read-only default permissions)
items.title: Make the GITHUB_TOKEN read-only
items.short: Make GITHUB_TOKEN read-only by default and grant write access job by job.
items.why: Every job gets a GITHUB_TOKEN, and any code that runs in the job can usually get at it. In the April 2026 Elementary attack, a command injected through a PR comment used the workflow's own token to trigger a malicious release. ImageMagick found its older repositories still gave workflows write access to contents, packages, pull requests and more, when most needed only contents: read.
steps: Set the repository default to read-only and stop Actions from approving pull requests. If you have an organization, set it there too; Mockoon locked down both levels.
Put permissions: {} at the top of every workflow file, as virtualenv recommends, so each job starts with no access.
Grant scopes in the job that uses them: contents: read to check out, contents: write only where a release is created, id-token: write only in the publish job.
Find gaps with zizmor's excessive-permissions audit or CodeQL's "Workflow does not contain permissions" query. evcc used GitHubSecurityLab/actions-permissions to work out what each job needs.
Run each workflow once after the change and add back only the scopes that actually fail.

snippets.label: Deny by default, grant per job
snippets.code:
name: CI
on:
  push:
    branches: [{branch}]
    tags: ["v*"]
  pull_request:

# Jobs start with no token permissions and ask for what they need
permissions: {}

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - run: make test

  github-release:
    if: startsWith(github.ref, 'refs/tags/v')
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: write   # the only job that can write
    steps:
      - env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          TAG: ${{ github.ref_name }}
        run: gh release create "$TAG" --repo "$GITHUB_REPOSITORY" --generate-notes

pitfalls: A permissions block inside one job doesn't limit the others. Fastify calls this the detail people get wrong most often: one forgotten job keeps its write token.
Listing any permission sets every unlisted one to none, so a job can fail until you add the scope it uses, such as pull-requests: write for a labeler.
Changing the default doesn't touch workflows that already ask for more (write-all or explicit write scopes). Search for those too.

items.label: Pin actions to full commit SHAs (and keep them updated)
items.title: Pin actions to full commit SHAs
items.short: Pin every action to a full commit SHA and let Dependabot keep the pins current.
items.why: A tag like @v4 can be moved to different code by the action's owner, or by whoever compromises them. In March 2025 attackers repointed the tags of tj-actions/changed-files, used by more than 20,000 repositories, so workflows dumped their CI secrets into build logs. Repositories pinned to a commit SHA largely ran the code they had reviewed.
steps: Pin existing workflows with a tool: pinact run, or frizbee actions .github/workflows/. Both keep the version as a comment Dependabot understands; ratchet works too, with its own update command.
Pin GitHub's own actions and reusable workflows from other repositories too, as Fastify did for actions/* and its fastify/workflows repository.
Add the Dependabot config below. Its pull requests bump both the SHA and the version comment, so pins move forward through review.
Turn on "Require actions to be pinned to a full-length commit SHA" in the Actions settings so a new unpinned uses: line fails instead of slipping in.
Read the changes in each bump before merging, especially for small actions with a single maintainer.
To also pin the actions your actions call, look at GitHub's workflow lockfile (gh actions-lock). actix-web adopted it and notes it is still experimental, with trade-offs.

snippets.label: What pinned steps look like
snippets.code:
steps:
  # Full 40-character commit SHA, version kept as a trailing comment.
  # Dependabot updates both when a new release comes out.
  - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
    with:
      persist-credentials: false
  - uses: actions/setup-python@6d4fd22b20465ccc0f7354476588e8df7c9ca0e0 # v7.1.0
    with:
      python-version: "3.x"

snippets.label: .github/dependabot.yml: keep action pins fresh
snippets.code:
version: 2
updates:
  - package-ecosystem: "github-actions"
    directory: "/"
    schedule:
      interval: "weekly"
    cooldown:
      default-days: 7   # skip releases younger than a week, as Gitoxide does

pitfalls: Dependabot alerts skip actions pinned to a SHA; only version updates move them. Without the github-actions entry in dependabot.yml, pins quietly go stale.
A SHA pin covers only the action you name. A composite action can still call other actions by tag, and a Docker action can pull an image by tag.
Take the SHA from the action's own repository, not a fork. A fork's commit can be referenced through the parent's name; zizmor's impostor-commit audit checks for this.

items.label: Avoid script injection (no untrusted ${{ }} in run steps)
items.title: Keep untrusted input out of run steps
items.short: Pass event data into run steps through env variables, never inline ${{ }}.
items.why: GitHub pastes ${{ }} expressions into the script before the shell runs it, so a PR title, branch name or comment can turn into a command. It hurts most in workflows triggered by issues, comments, pull_request_target or workflow_run, which run with your secrets and token. In April 2026 a PR comment was substituted into an Elementary workflow script, and the attacker used the workflow token to ship a malicious release that stayed on PyPI for 11.5 hours.
steps: Search workflows and composite actions for ${{ inside run: blocks, especially titles, bodies, comments, head_ref and inputs. zizmor's template-injection audit lists them.
Move each value into the step's env: block and use "$VAR" in the script. zizmor --fix can rewrite some of them for you.
In actions/github-script, read process.env.VAR instead of pasting ${{ }} into the JavaScript, as JUnit did in its release workflow.
Treat step outputs built from PR data as untrusted too. ACI.dev's CodeQL code-injection alert came from a PR title passed through a step output.
Don't write unvalidated input to $GITHUB_ENV or $GITHUB_OUTPUT; a newline in the value can define extra variables or outputs.
Keep zizmor or CodeQL in CI so new injections show up in review.

items.label: Remove or guard pull_request_target / workflow_run / issue_comment triggers
items.title: Remove or isolate pull_request_target
items.short: Use pull_request instead of pull_request_target, or split off the privileged steps.
items.why: pull_request_target and workflow_run run with your repository's token and secrets, so checking out and building a pull request's code there hands both to whoever opened it. ImageMagick's maintainer found this mistake in an editor extension with millions of installs. GitHub's new default event policy blocks pull_request_target in public repositories, with enforcement starting December 2, 2026.
steps: Find workflows triggered by pull_request_target, workflow_run or issue_comment. zizmor's dangerous-triggers audit lists them; Policy insights under Settings → Actions → Policies shows runs the new default would block.
If a job only builds and tests, switch it to pull_request, as ACI.dev did for its backend checks.
If it must write (comment, label, publish results), split it: a pull_request workflow runs the code read-only, and a workflow_run workflow posts the results without checking out PR code.

In the privileged half, treat everything from the PR as data: validate artifact contents and keep them out of scripts and $GITHUB_ENV. fabric.js stopped reading the PR number from an uploaded artifact.
Replace comment-triggered commands with labels that only maintainers can add, as Node.js recommends.
Fix or delete old branches too. pull_request_target uses the workflow file from the PR's target branch, so a stale branch keeps an old hole open.

name: PR tests

permissions:

      # Hand the privileged workflow data, never code
      - name: Save PR number
        if: always()
        env:
          PR_NUMBER: ${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}

      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@cf430e030ddbb5b0abf93d22962f4752f3646cd9 # v7.0.2

snippets.code:
# Can write to the PR, but never checks out or runs PR code
name: PR comment
on:
  workflow_run:
    workflows: ["PR tests"]
    types: [completed]

permissions: {}

jobs:
  comment:
    if: github.event.workflow_run.event == 'pull_request'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      actions: read          # download the other run's artifact
      pull-requests: write   # post the comment
    steps:
      # The artifact came from the PR, so it is untrusted data
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@9000827ccba6bdab643e8b6fd33ac0654aef8333 # v8.0.2
        with:
          name: pr-number
          run-id: ${{ github.event.workflow_run.id }}
          github-token: ${{ github.token }}
          path: ${{ runner.temp }}/pr
      - name: Comment with the result
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          GH_REPO: ${{ github.repository }}
          RESULT: ${{ github.event.workflow_run.conclusion }}
        run: |
          pr="$(cat "$RUNNER_TEMP/pr/pr-number")"
          [[ "$pr" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || { echo "Unexpected PR number"; exit 1; }
          gh pr comment "$pr" --body "Tests finished: $RESULT"

items.label: Don't persist git credentials after checkout
items.title: Don't leave the token in .git/config
items.short: Set persist-credentials: false on every actions/checkout step.
items.why: By default actions/checkout stores the job's token on disk so later git commands work, which also lets every later step, test script and build tool read it. Gitoxide turned it off because its tests work on the checked-out repository, and a test could otherwise leak the token.
steps: Add with: persist-credentials: false to every actions/checkout step. zizmor's artipacked audit lists any you missed.
Where a job really pushes (a changelog commit, a tag), set persist-credentials: true explicitly in that job only, with a comment saying why.
Keep that pushing job small and separate from jobs that run tests or third-party tools.
Don't upload the whole workspace or $RUNNER_TEMP as an artifact.
Optionally add a CI check that fails when a checkout step lacks the setting. Gitoxide runs a check-no-persist-credentials job.

snippets.label: Off by default, explicit where a job pushes
snippets.code:
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false   # no token left on disk
      - run: make test

  update-changelog:
    if: github.event_name == 'push'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: true    # this job pushes; say so
      - run: ./scripts/commit-changelog.sh   # commits and runs git push

pitfalls: actions/checkout v6 and later keep the credential in a file under $RUNNER_TEMP instead of .git/config, but git still uses it automatically, so the setting still matters.
Turning it off breaks later steps that git push, push tags or fetch from private repositories. Give those jobs their own explicit setting instead of turning it back on everywhere.

items.title: Lint workflows with zizmor
items.short: Run zizmor on your workflows, fix what it finds, and keep it running in CI.
items.why: Workflow mistakes such as template injection, dangerous triggers, unpinned actions, stored credentials and broad permissions are hard to spot by eye and easy to find with a static checker. virtualenv's maintainer notes that zizmor catches template injection like the one behind the April 2026 Elementary attack.

items.label: Audit, scope and rotate CI secrets; use environments
items.title: Scope, rotate and retire CI secrets
items.short: List your CI secrets, delete unused ones, scope the rest to environments, and rotate.
items.why: Any secret a workflow can reach is one compromised step away from an attacker. In March 2026 an unpinned scanner in LiteLLM's release pipeline could read its static release secrets, including the PyPI credential, and the malicious releases that followed got over 119,000 downloads in two and a half hours. kgateway removed unused secrets from its environments during the program, and shadcn/ui audited every workflow secret.
steps: List every repository, environment and organization secret with the workflow that uses it. Delete anything nothing uses.
Replace registry and cloud tokens with trusted publishing or OIDC where you can, then delete them. ScanCode removed its PyPI token after switching.
Move the secrets you keep into an environment, such as release, so only jobs that name it, and pass its rules, can read them.
Pass each secret only to the step that uses it, and name secrets explicitly when calling a reusable workflow instead of using secrets: inherit.
Use fine-grained tokens with only the permissions they need, as Sniffnet recommends, limited to one repository and with an expiry date.
Keep admin-level tokens out of CI. Fastify runs its org-admin scripts from a maintainer's laptop with a temporary token.

snippets.label: Environment-scoped secret, passed to one step
snippets.code:
jobs:
  deploy-docs:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: docs      # the secret is stored on this environment
    permissions:
      contents: read
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - name: Upload docs
        env:
          DOCS_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.DOCS_TOKEN }}   # only this step sees it
        run: ./scripts/upload-docs.sh

  release:
    uses: ./.github/workflows/release.yml
    secrets:
      SIGNING_KEY: ${{ secrets.SIGNING_KEY }}   # instead of secrets: inherit

pitfalls: Deleting a secret from GitHub doesn't revoke it. Revoke it at the registry or service too, or any leaked copy keeps working.
Log masking isn't guaranteed once a value is transformed (base64, URL-encoded). Don't print secrets or anything derived from them.
When someone with admin access leaves, rotate the secrets they could see.

items.label: Use OIDC / short-lived credentials instead of long-lived tokens
items.title: Use OIDC instead of long-lived tokens
items.short: Swap long-lived cloud and service tokens for short-lived OIDC credentials.
items.why: A token stored as a secret works for anyone who gets a copy until you revoke it. With OIDC the job proves which repository, branch and environment it runs in, and gets a credential that expires with the job. It isn't only for publishing: mimetype moved its Codecov uploads to OIDC.
steps: List secrets that hold keys for clouds, registries or services, and check which providers accept GitHub's OIDC tokens: package registries, AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Vault, Codecov and others.
On the provider, trust only your repository and pin the subject to a branch, tag or environment, such as repo:{owner}/{repo}:environment:release.
Give id-token: write only to the job that exchanges the token, ideally one bound to a protected environment.
Switch the step to the provider's OIDC login, such as aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials with role-to-assume, or codecov-action with use_oidc: true.
Delete the old secret from GitHub and revoke the key at the provider.

snippets.code:
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production   # the role trusts only this environment
    permissions:
      contents: read
      id-token: write         # lets this job request an OIDC token
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@e1253824e5c10ff9df46874f81ed3ec929e19cfd # v6.3.0
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/{repo}-deploy
          aws-region: us-east-1
      - run: aws s3 sync site/ s3://example-bucket/

pitfalls: A trust policy that accepts repo:{owner}/{repo}:* lets any branch or pull request workflow in the repository assume the role. Match a specific environment or ref.
Repositories created after July 15, 2026, or opted in, get a subject with numeric IDs (repo:octo-org@123456/octo-repo@456789:...). Write the trust policy for the format your repository uses.
Pull requests from forks can't get OIDC tokens, so jobs that need one should run on push, tag or environment-gated events.

items.label: Harden runners (egress control, e.g. harden-runner)
items.title: Restrict what your runners can reach
items.short: Limit the hosts CI jobs can reach, and keep public PRs off self-hosted runners.
items.why: When a compromised dependency or action runs in your job, its next move is usually to send your token or secrets to a server it controls. virtualenv's maintainer lists restricting the hosts a build can reach as baseline hardening.
steps: Add harden-runner as the first step of jobs that hold secrets or publish, with egress-policy: audit.
After a few runs, open the insights link in the job summary and note the endpoints each job really calls.
Switch to egress-policy: block with that list in allowed-endpoints. A blocked call then fails the job and names the endpoint for you to review.
Use GitHub-hosted runners for public repositories. GitHub says self-hosted runners should almost never be used there, since anyone who opens a pull request can run code on them.
If you must self-host, use ephemeral just-in-time runners that run one job, start clean and can't reach internal networks.

snippets.label: Block egress except an allowlist
snippets.code:
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
    steps:
      # Must be the first step in the job
      - uses: step-security/harden-runner@46b06cea07f9e64621fdf066ba77ac6915163d43 # v2.22.3
        with:
          egress-policy: block   # start with audit, then switch
          allowed-endpoints: >
            github.com:443
            api.github.com:443
            registry.npmjs.org:443
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - run: npm ci && npm test

pitfalls: harden-runner's free tier covers public repositories on GitHub-hosted runners, and block mode works on Linux only. Private repositories and self-hosted runners need StepSecurity's paid tier.

An allowlist still permits the hosts on it, and an attacker with their own token can send data to github.com. Egress control narrows the way out and makes attempts visible; it doesn't close every path.

items.label: Require approval before running workflows from first-time contributors
items.title: Approve first-time contributors' workflow runs
items.short: Require approval before workflows run on pull requests from new contributors.
items.why: If a stranger's pull request runs automatically, their code, including any edited workflow files, executes on your runners before anyone has looked at it. steps: In the Actions settings, check "Approval for running fork pull request workflows from contributors" is at least "Require approval for first-time contributors", GitHub's current default.
Choose "Require approval for all external contributors" if you use self-hosted runners or get many drive-by PRs from new accounts.

items.label: Don't trust caches or artifacts across trust boundaries (no shared caches in release jobs)
items.title: Don't trust caches or artifacts in release jobs
items.short: Don't restore caches in release jobs, and treat downloaded artifacts as untrusted.
items.why: GitHub doesn't sign or verify cache contents, and an artifact from a pull request run holds whatever the PR author wanted, so restoring either in a release job lets lower-trust code into the job that holds your publishing credentials. virtualenv's maintainer lists "don't restore shared caches in the release job" as baseline hardening, and fabric.js stopped its privileged workflow_run job from reading the PR number out of an uploaded artifact.
steps: Set cache-mode: none on release and publish jobs, or on the whole release workflow, so they neither restore nor save Actions caches.
Turn off caching built into setup actions there too, for example package-manager-cache: false on setup-node or enable-cache: false on setup-uv.
Build release artifacts inside the release workflow from the tagged commit. Don't promote artifacts produced by pull request runs.
In workflow_run jobs, download artifacts into $RUNNER_TEMP, never execute them, and validate every value before use, such as checking a PR number is only digits.
Keep cache writes in trusted push or schedule workflows. pull_request_target and workflow_run now get read-only cache access by default; don't override that with cache-mode: write.

snippets.label: Release job that uses no cache
snippets.code:
jobs:
  release:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    cache-mode: none   # don't restore or save any Actions cache
    environment: release
    permissions:
      contents: read
      id-token: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: actions/setup-node@949feb2413d6458794dcd2491c4babbbce0c15c1 # v7.1.0
        with:
          node-version: "24"
          registry-url: "https://registry.npmjs.org"
          package-manager-cache: false   # setup-node caches by default
      - run: npm ci && npm run build --if-present
      - run: npm publish

snippets.label: Reading a value from an artifact in a workflow_run job
snippets.code:
- name: Read PR number (untrusted)
  id: pr
  run: |
    pr="$(cat "$RUNNER_TEMP/pr/pr-number")"
    [[ "$pr" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || { echo "Unexpected value"; exit 1; }
    echo "number=$pr" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

pitfalls: Third-party caching actions only honor cache-mode if they use GitHub's cache toolkit. Turn off their own cache input in release jobs as well.
Cache-free release builds are slower. That's the expected trade-off; npm's own trusted publishing example says never to use caching in release builds.
Linters can lag behind: actionlint 1.7.12 reports cache-mode as an unknown key, though GitHub accepts it.

items.label: Run CodeQL code scanning on every PR
items.title: Run CodeQL on every pull request
items.short: Turn on CodeQL code scanning so changes are checked before they merge.
items.why: CodeQL follows untrusted input to dangerous calls such as SQL queries, shell commands, deserializers and HTML output, and it's free for public repositories. shadcn/ui's first scan caught an unsafe dangerouslySetInnerHTML path, and CocoIndex says CodeQL already catches issues that manual review missed.
steps: Go to Settings → Advanced Security (Code security on some accounts). In the CodeQL analysis row, choose Set up → Default. There's no workflow file to maintain.
Before enabling, click Edit: pick the Extended query suite and keep GitHub Actions in the language list.
Check that every language you ship is listed. SciPy scans both its Python and its C code.
Default setup skips pull requests from forks, so it only sees that code after merge. If most contributions come from forks, use advanced setup (below) instead.
Make findings block merges: Settings → Rulesets → New branch ruleset → Require code scanning results, with CodeQL set to High or higher.

snippets.label: Advanced setup, which also scans fork PRs: .github/workflows/codeql.yml
snippets.code:
name: CodeQL
on:
  push:
    branches: [{branch}]
  pull_request:
    branches: [{branch}]
  schedule:
    - cron: '30 4 * * 1'

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  analyze:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      security-events: write
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        # Your languages: actions, c-cpp, csharp, go, java-kotlin,
        # javascript-typescript, python, ruby, rust, swift.
        # Compiled languages may also need a build-mode (see the docs).
        language: [actions, python]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: github/codeql-action/init@9b3254085494b55a0f7c4c2b3d2d52cc712ce370 # v4.39.1
        with:
          languages: ${{ matrix.language }}
          queries: security-extended
      - uses: github/codeql-action/analyze@9b3254085494b55a0f7c4c2b3d2d52cc712ce370 # v4.39.1
        with:
          category: /language:${{ matrix.language }}

items.label: Write custom CodeQL queries or packs
items.title: Write custom CodeQL queries
items.short: Write CodeQL queries for the bug patterns and risky calls specific to your project.
items.why: The built-in queries know common frameworks, not your own helpers and danger spots. DocsGPT's custom queries inventory every untrusted-input point and dangerous sink, so new attack surface has to be allow-listed on purpose, and Log4j is building a CodeQL pack that flags unsafe logging patterns in downstream code.
steps: Budget a few days to learn QL. Start from a real bug: after a fix, write a query that finds the same pattern elsewhere (variant analysis).
Or write inventory queries that flag every risky call (eval, shell, deserializers, raw SQL), so each new one gets a review, as DocsGPT does.
Prototype in VS Code with the CodeQL extension, then keep the query in an in-repo pack (codeql pack init creates the qlpack.yml).
Run it through a config file in advanced setup (config-file on the init step). Org-owned repos can also attach one to default setup with the github-codeql-config-file property.
Add sample code that should and shouldn't match, and run codeql test run in CI so the query keeps working.
If CodeQL misses flows through your own wrapper library, a model pack that describes its sources and sinks may be simpler than a new query.

snippets.code:
/**
 * @name Unpickling call
 * @description pickle can run code from its input. Each call needs a check that the data is trusted.
 * @kind problem
 * @problem.severity warning
 * @security-severity 7.0
 * @id py/project-pickle-load
 * @tags security
 */

import python
import semmle.python.ApiGraphs

from API::CallNode call
where call = API::moduleImport("pickle").getMember(["load", "loads"]).getACall()
select call, "pickle runs code from its input. Confirm this data can't come from users."

items.label: Use Copilot Autofix on code scanning alerts
items.title: Fix alerts faster with Copilot Autofix
items.short: Use Copilot Autofix to draft fixes for CodeQL alerts, and review each one.
items.why: An alert nobody fixes protects no one. With CodeQL on, Copilot Autofix suggests a code change and an explanation for many alerts, at no cost on public repositories. Cucumber automated fix generation for CodeQL and secret scanning findings across more than 130 repositories.
steps: There's nothing to install: with CodeQL enabled, Autofix suggestions appear as comments on pull requests that introduce supported alerts.
For existing alerts, open the Security and quality tab → Code scanning, pick an alert, click Generate fix, then Create PR with fix.
Or select up to 25 alerts and click Assign to Copilot for a draft PR (agentic autofix). An admin turns it on, and it uses Actions minutes and AI credits.
Review every fix like a contributor's PR: does it close the hole without changing behavior? Run the tests and add a regression test.
If a suggestion looks wrong, don't merge it. Fix it by hand, or dismiss the alert with a reason and a comment.
pitfalls: Autofix is best effort and can't fix every alert. Agentic autofix can't validate fixes for custom queries, the Extended suite or other tools' alerts.
Merging fixes you don't understand. A change that silences the query but leaves the bug is worse than an open alert.

items.short: Work through open code scanning alerts: fix real bugs, dismiss noise with a reason.

Book a recurring slot, such as an hour a week, and track the count. DataJourney logged 50+ resolved findings by its 12-month check-in.
Stop new debt from piling up by requiring code scanning results in a branch ruleset.

items.label: Enroll in Anthropic's OSS Scanner (vulnerability reports straight from its models)
items.title: Enroll in Anthropic's OSS Scanner
items.short: Let Anthropic's models scan your code for free, if you can handle unreviewed reports.
items.why: OSS Scanner scans enrolled open source projects with Anthropic's strongest models at no cost, emails each report straight from the models (unreviewed, with a reproducer and a proposed patch where there is one) and rescans regularly; projects that aren't enrolled only get findings after human review through Anthropic's coordinated disclosure process, which is slower. Anthropic decides who joins case by case, with criteria like OSS-Fuzz's, and brand-new projects and forks usually don't qualify. This guide suggests checking once a project has over 1,000 stars or 200 dependents, but that cue is this guide's, not Anthropic's rule.
steps: Decide whether you can keep up. Reports arrive unreviewed, and Anthropic built this for projects already handling verified high and critical reports. Without it, you get only human-reviewed findings.
Add .oss-scanner/Dockerfile: it must install every dependency and build the project, because the scan runs with no network. Build it and run your tests inside with --network none (below).

Optionally add .oss-scanner/threat_model.md (anthropics/oss-scanner has a template): what's in scope, where untrusted input enters, and how you rate severity, such as whether post-auth SQL injection is high or critical.
As a core maintainer, run tools/validate.py and tools/check <name>, then open the pull request adding projects/<name>/project.yaml (below; a lowercase name) with your published security contact.
Optional: to get reports on GitHub too, turn on private vulnerability reporting, add the oss-scanner account as a trusted reporter, and set output_format.github_security_advisory.min_severity.
To pause reports, set disabled: true in a pull request; to leave, delete projects/<name>/. Either way you're back to reviewed findings only.

Check the image the way the scanner uses it, from your repository root
snippets.code:
docker build -f .oss-scanner/Dockerfile -t oss-scanner-test .
# The checkout is at /src; use your own test command.
docker run --rm --network none oss-scanner-test sh -c 'cd /src && make test'

pitfalls: Reports aren't reviewed by a human, so some are false positives, and the first scan sends a bundle at once. Decide who triages them before you enroll.
Every email address in project.yaml is public, and Anthropic checks that primary_contact is a security contact you publish, for example in SECURITY.md. Use a security alias, not a personal address.
pgp can't be combined with auto_ccs: encrypted email goes to primary_contact only, and GitHub reports aren't encrypted.

items.label: Enable secret scanning (and/or gitleaks/trufflehog)
items.title: Turn on secret scanning
items.short: Turn on secret scanning so leaked keys in your code and history raise an alert.
items.why: GitHub Security Lab cites 28.65 million new secrets leaked on public GitHub in 2025, with AI-assisted commits leaking them at about twice the usual rate. Secret scanning checks your entire Git history plus issues, PRs, discussions and wikis, and it's free on public repos. Cucumber used it to drive fixes across more than 130 repositories.
steps: Settings → Advanced Security (in the "Security and quality" section; "Code security" on some accounts) → Secret Protection → Enable.
Turn on push protection on the same page, so new leaks are blocked before they land.
Check open alerts in the repo's Security tab under Secret scanning, and watch the repo for security alerts so you hear about new ones.
Treat every real alert as a leak: rotate the secret first, then close the alert as revoked.
For many repos, use an org security configuration or the loop below; Mockoon turned it on for all of its repositories.
Optionally add a scanner such as gitleaks in CI or pre-commit, as GoReleaser does, to catch formats GitHub doesn't recognize.

snippets.label: Turn on secret scanning and push protection for every public repo you own
snippets.code:
gh repo list {owner} --visibility public --no-archived --source --limit 1000 \
  --json nameWithOwner --jq '.[].nameWithOwner' |
while read -r r; do
  gh api -X PATCH "repos/$r" --silent -f 'security_and_analysis[secret_scanning][status]=enabled' &&
  gh api -X PATCH "repos/$r" --silent -f 'security_and_analysis[secret_scanning_push_protection][status]=enabled' &&
  echo "on: $r"
done

pitfalls: Deleting the commit neither closes the alert nor un-leaks the key. Alerts stay open until you resolve them.
Private repos in an org need a paid Secret Protection license; public repos don't.

items.label: Enable push protection
items.title: Block secrets before they're pushed
items.short: Turn on push protection so pushes containing secrets are rejected before they land.
items.why: Once a key is pushed you have to assume it's stolen and rotate it; a blocked push costs you a minute. Your personal "push protection for users" already blocks supported secrets in your own pushes to public repos, but only repo-level push protection covers every contributor and raises an alert when someone bypasses it.
steps: Settings → Advanced Security → in the Secret Protection section, click Enable next to "Push protection".
When a push is blocked, remove the secret from every commit it appears in (snippet below) instead of bypassing.
Move real secrets into environment variables or your CI's secret store, and add .env files to .gitignore.
Check bypasses: each one creates an alert and emails admins. "I'll fix it later" leaves an open alert for a real secret, so rotate it.
In an org, consider delegated bypass, so only named people can approve pushing a flagged secret.

snippets.label: Unblock a push by removing the secret from your commits
snippets.code:
# Secret is in your latest commit: delete it from the file, then
git commit --amend --all
git push

# Secret is in an earlier commit (the push error lists every commit that has it)
git rebase -i <EARLIEST-COMMIT>~1   # change "pick" to "edit" for that commit
# ...delete the secret from the file, then:
git add .
git commit --amend
git rebase --continue
git push

pitfalls: "It's used in tests" and "It's a false positive" bypasses create alerts that are already closed. Make sure the key really isn't live.
Push protection only knows supported patterns. It won't catch every password or homemade token.

items.label: Rotate leaked secrets and clean them up
items.title: Rotate any leaked secret first, then clean up
items.short: If a secret leaks, revoke and replace it first; cleaning up Git history comes later.
items.why: A pushed secret is compromised the moment it's public: copies live on in clones, forks, caches and PR refs, so deleting the commit protects nothing. In the Ultralytics attack, the later malicious PyPI uploads came through an old API token, which is why every credential that could have been exposed needs revoking, not just the one you spotted.
steps: Revoke or rotate the secret at the provider now: create a replacement, update CI and deployments, then revoke the old one.
Check the provider's logs and your registry's release history for anything done with the old credential since it leaked.
Rotate anything stored next to it, such as other secrets in the same CI environment, and any token you can't account for.
Close the secret scanning alert as revoked, with a note (snippet below).

Only then decide about history. Once the secret is revoked, rewriting is usually unnecessary; for sensitive data, use git-filter-repo --sensitive-data-removal and ask GitHub Support to purge cached views.
Prevent a repeat: push protection, env files in .gitignore, OIDC instead of stored tokens. Two.js treats anything pasted into an AI chat as public.

snippets.label: List open secret scanning alerts, then close one as revoked
snippets.code:
gh api "repos/{owner}/{repo}/secret-scanning/alerts?state=open" \
  --jq '.[] | "\(.number)\t\(.secret_type_display_name)\t\(.created_at)"'

# After revoking the secret at the provider:
gh api -X PATCH "repos/{owner}/{repo}/secret-scanning/alerts/<number>" \
  -f state=resolved -f resolution=revoked \
  -f resolution_comment="Revoked and replaced on YYYY-MM-DD; provider logs checked"

pitfalls: Rewriting history before revoking: anyone with an old clone notices the rewrite, which points them at what you removed while the key still works.
Rotating only the token you found. Look for older tokens and keys with the same reach.

items.title: Automate dependency updates (actions too)
