Keep the cooldown (7 days in the template) so you don't pick up a release in its riskiest first days.

Prefer Renovate if you need more control, such as custom managers or schedules. oapi-codegen uses it for Go modules and Actions.

items.label: Dependency review on pull requests
items.title: Review new dependencies in pull requests
items.short: Check what each pull request adds to your dependencies before you merge it.
items.why: A pull request can add a vulnerable or malicious package in a lockfile diff nobody reads. Dependency review lists what a PR adds or upgrades and flags known advisories; GitHub says it turns an opaque package.json diff into a two-minute review.

Add the workflow from the template and make it a required status check in your branch ruleset.

Read lockfile diffs for new transitive packages too, not just the manifest.
pitfalls: It only knows published advisories, so a brand-new malicious package passes. Pair it with a cooldown.
Ecosystems the dependency graph can't parse are invisible to it. Submit them with dependency submission.
deny-licenses is deprecated; use allow-licenses.

items.label: Use a dependency cooldown (wait days before adopting new releases)
items.title: Wait a few days before adopting new releases
items.short: Wait a few days before adopting new releases, in your update bot and your installer.
items.why: Malicious releases are usually spotted and pulled within hours or days, so most of the risk is in being among the first to install. After the Shai-Hulud worm, Fastify's npm installs only take versions older than 2 days; CPython's Dependabot waits 14 days, and Gitoxide 7 days for Cargo and Actions.
steps: Dependabot: add cooldown to each ecosystem. It already waits 3 days by default; 7 is a common choice. Security updates are never delayed.
Renovate: set minimumReleaseAge, such as "7 days". With the default internalChecksFilter "strict", younger versions get no PR; vulnerability fixes skip the wait.
npm 11.10 or later: put min-release-age=<days> in the project .npmrc (Fastify uses 2). pnpm: minimumReleaseAge in pnpm-workspace.yaml, counted in minutes.
Python: set exclude-newer = "7 days" under [tool.uv], or pass --uploaded-prior-to P7D to pip, as virtualenv's maintainer recommends.
Exempt your own packages or an urgent fix explicitly: Dependabot exclude (Node.js exempts its own doc-kit), npm min-release-age-exclude, uv exclude-newer-package.
If you run zizmor, its dependabot-cooldown audit flags Dependabot configs with no or a short cooldown.

updates:

    schedule:

      default-days: 7
      semver-major-days: 14
      exclude:
        - "my-own-package"   # releases you trust can skip the wait

Renovate needs release timestamps. Dependencies without them never age in, so exempt them as Pillow does for google/oss-fuzz.

items.label: Disable package install/lifecycle scripts by default
items.title: Disable npm install scripts
items.short: Stop dependencies from running install scripts, and allow only the few that need them.
items.why: In September 2025 the Shai-Hulud worm spread through npm install scripts, running on developers' machines with their credentials in reach. Fastify added ignore-scripts=true to its repositories' .npmrc; its test suites never needed those hooks, so it cost nothing.
steps: Check npm -v. npm 12 already blocks dependency install scripts unless the allowScripts list in package.json approves them; approve with npm approve-scripts <pkg>.
On npm 11 or older, commit the .npmrc from the template so every clone and CI run skips dependency scripts.
Run your build and tests. For a package that needs a native build (Fastify's example is sharp), run npm rebuild <pkg> --ignore-scripts=false after installing.
In CI, install with npm ci so you get exactly the lockfile, with the committed .npmrc applied.
pnpm 10 and later skip dependency build scripts until you approve them (pnpm approve-builds); Bun runs them only for trustedDependencies and its built-in list; in Yarn, set enableScripts: false.

npm rebuild sharp --ignore-scripts=false

# npm 12: scripts are blocked until approved in package.json "allowScripts"
npm approve-scripts sharp   # writes a version-pinned approval
npm rebuild sharp

pitfalls: ignore-scripts also skips your own lifecycle scripts, such as a prepare script that installs git hooks, and the pre/post scripts around npm test.
With ignore-scripts in .npmrc, a plain npm rebuild <pkg> runs nothing; add --ignore-scripts=false. It also overrides npm 12 approvals.
Code that runs when a package is imported still runs. Pair this with a cooldown and dependency review.

items.label: Remove unused or risky dependencies; shrink the dependency surface
items.title: Remove dependencies you don't need
items.short: Remove dependencies you don't need; every one is code you're trusting.
items.why: Every package brings code, maintainers and install-time hooks you trust on your users' behalf. OpenClaw moved features into plugins for a shorter dependency tree and a smaller attack surface.
steps: List what you ship, direct and transitive (npm ls --all, uv tree, cargo tree, go mod graph), and note which are runtime and which are dev-only.
Find unused ones with a tool: knip (JavaScript/TypeScript), deptry (Python), cargo-machete (Rust), go mod tidy (Go).
Ask why each remaining one is there (npm explain, uv tree --invert --package, cargo tree -i, go mod why -m), and replace tiny ones with your own code.
Move optional features behind extras or plugins so the core install stays small, as OpenClaw did.
Make each new dependency a reviewed decision with a reason in the PR. CocoIndex tracks what it depends on and why.

uvx deptry .                                     # Python

items.title: Check dependency licenses
items.short: Check in CI that dependency licenses are compatible with your project's license.

items.label: Lock and hash-pin dependencies
items.title: Commit lockfiles
items.short: Commit lockfiles, with hashes where you can, and install from them exactly in CI.
items.why: A lockfile records the exact versions, and usually hashes, that you tested, so CI and contributors can't silently pick up a new or tampered release. virtualenv found it was downloading pip and setuptools updates without checking hashes; with hash pinning, even a one-character change to a wheel is rejected.
steps: Commit the lockfile for your ecosystem: package-lock.json, pnpm-lock.yaml, yarn.lock, uv.lock or pylock.toml, Cargo.lock, go.sum.
Install strictly from it in CI: npm ci, pnpm install --frozen-lockfile, uv sync --locked, cargo build --locked. Go checks downloads against go.sum.
For pip, add hashes: generate them with uv pip compile --generate-hashes or pip-tools, and install with --require-hashes.
Lock your release and build tools too, not just runtime dependencies.
Review lockfile diffs in PRs: new packages, changed registry URLs, and hashes that change without a version bump.

snippets.label: Install exactly what's locked (CI)
snippets.code:
npm ci                                    # fails if package-lock.json doesn't match package.json
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
uv sync --locked                          # fails if uv.lock is out of date
cargo build --locked
go mod verify                             # checks the module cache against go.sum
pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt

pitfalls: Expecting a library's lockfile to protect users. They resolve from your version ranges; Cargo's FAQ says the lockfile doesn't affect your package's consumers.
Running npm install in CI. It rewrites the lockfile instead of failing on drift; use npm ci.
Waving through contributor lockfile changes. A swapped resolved URL can point at a different tarball.

items.label: Generate SBOMs for releases
items.title: Ship an SBOM with releases
items.short: Generate an SBOM for each release and attach it to the release.
items.why: When an advisory lands, an SBOM answers "are we affected?" for you and your users, including code you bundle or vendor that a dependency listing misses. virtualenv embeds one in its wheel (PEP 770) because it bundles pip and setuptools, which vendor their own dependencies. DocsGPT found exporting one from GitHub was "a button, not a project".
steps: Start with the free export: Insights → Dependency graph → Export SBOM gives an SPDX file of your declared dependencies.
For what you actually ship, generate an SBOM in the release workflow from the build output or container image, for example with Syft (GoReleaser's suggestion) through anchore/sbom-action.
Attach it to the draft release before publishing; with immutable releases on, assets can't be added later. TokenOps attaches a CycloneDX SBOM to every release.
Make vendored code visible. aiohttp submits its vendored llhttp to the dependency graph on every push, so it appears in the SBOM and gets Dependabot alerts.
Optionally sign it: actions/attest with sbom-path ties the SBOM to the artifact it describes.

snippets.label: Generate an SBOM and attach it to the draft release
snippets.code:
jobs:
  sbom:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: write   # attach the file to the draft release
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - run: make dist   # build what you ship first
      - uses: anchore/sbom-action@66cbf4bc1f1c0d2edc94016e65bc221b6bb0ad6c # v0.24.3
        with:
          format: spdx-json
          output-file: sbom.spdx.json
          upload-release-assets: false   # attached below instead
      - name: Attach to the draft release
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          TAG: ${{ github.ref_name }}
        run: gh release upload "$TAG" sbom.spdx.json --repo "$GITHUB_REPOSITORY"

pitfalls: GitHub's exported SBOM reflects your manifests and lock files, not what's compiled into a binary or vendored into your package.
Keep build-machine details out. virtualenv's rebuilds didn't match until it removed them from the SBOM in its wheel.
Regenerate it for every release; an SBOM for an older version answers the wrong question.

items.label: Publish build provenance attestations (SLSA)
items.title: Publish build provenance attestations
items.short: Publish signed build provenance for every release artifact.
items.why: Provenance records which repository, commit and workflow built a file, so users and investigators can tell your builds from impostors. In the Ultralytics attack, the later malicious uploads had no attestations, which told investigators they came through an old API token rather than the project's CI.
steps: Check what trusted publishing already gives you: PyPI's publish action uploads attestations by default, and npm adds provenance for public packages published from public repositories.
For release files and container images, add actions/attest after the build step, with id-token: write and attestations: write on that job only.
Attest the exact files you ship, then upload those same files. Rebuilding or re-zipping afterwards changes the digest.
Tell users how to check: gh attestation verify <file> -R {owner}/{repo}. Put it in the README or release notes.
For SLSA Build Level 3, run the build in a reusable workflow; attestations on their own give Build Level 2.

snippets.code:
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      id-token: write       # get a short-lived Sigstore signing certificate
      attestations: write   # store the attestation on GitHub
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - run: make dist      # your build; writes files to dist/
      - uses: actions/attest@1e69f48acb82d1966a394da916b4c1698aa569d6 # v4.2.2
        with:
          subject-path: "dist/*"
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@cf430e030ddbb5b0abf93d22962f4752f3646cd9 # v7.0.2
        with:
          name: dist
          path: dist/

items.label: Sign releases and artifacts (Sigstore/cosign/GPG)
items.title: Sign your releases
items.short: Sign release artifacts with Sigstore and tell users how to verify them.
items.why: A signature lets users and tools detect a swapped or tampered download, and keyless Sigstore signing ties it to your release workflow's identity, so there's no long-lived signing key to steal. Byte Buddy began signing its Maven deployments with Sigstore.
steps: Use what your registry already does: PyPI attestations and npm provenance are Sigstore-signed automatically with trusted publishing. Sign the rest (release files, binaries, images) yourself.
In the release job, install cosign and run cosign sign-blob --yes --bundle for each file. The job needs id-token: write.
Attach each .sigstore.json bundle to the draft release next to the file it signs, then publish.
Document the verify command, including your workflow's identity, in the README or SECURITY.md.
Sign your release tags too (git tag -s with a GPG or SSH key) so GitHub shows them as Verified.

items.label: Trusted publishing to registries (npm, PyPI, crates.io)
items.title: Use trusted publishing for your registry
items.short: Publish from CI with trusted publishing (OIDC), then delete your registry tokens.
items.why: A registry token in CI or on a laptop can publish as you until someone revokes it: stolen publishing tokens spread the Shai-Hulud worm, and in the Ultralytics attack the later malicious uploads came through an old API token. Trusted publishing replaces it with a token minted per run that expires in minutes (within 15 on PyPI, 30 on crates.io). Commits show more than 20 Fund teams switching to it during the program.
steps: Register a trusted publisher (owner, repo, workflow filename, environment) on the registry: PyPI project → Publishing, npm package Settings, crates.io crate Settings → Trusted Publishing, RubyGems gem page → Trusted publishers.
Build in one job without special permissions; publish in a separate job that has id-token: write and the matching environment: name.
Publish once to confirm it works, then delete the token secret from GitHub and revoke it on the registry. ScanCode and Foundry removed theirs.
On npm, set Publishing access to "Require two-factor authentication and disallow tokens" and revoke old automation tokens.
Protect what triggers the release: a tag ruleset for v* and, with more than one maintainer, required reviewers on the environment.
crates.io only: the first publish of a new crate still needs a normal API token. Switch after that.

items.label: Gate releases (two-person approval, protected environments, scripted steps)
items.title: Gate releases behind a protected environment
items.short: Put the publish job behind an environment that needs a human approval.
items.why: If any account with push access, or any compromised workflow, can start a release on its own, one stolen session or token is enough to ship malware under your name. OpenClaw now puts two people on every release, each one scripted, gated and signed off, and Fastify keeps a human on the publish button for its 50+ packages.

Under deployment branches and tags, allow only your release tags (v*) or your default branch.
Untick "Allow administrators to bypass configured protection rules".
Name the environment in the publish job and enter the same name in your trusted publisher, so the registry rejects publishes from elsewhere. Foundry added a release environment for npm.
Working alone? Make yourself the reviewer anyway; the pause makes you look before shipping. On npm, staged publishing adds a 2FA approval on npmjs.com before a version goes live.

steps: Pick a policy you can keep. For most solo projects, "latest release only" is honest and fine; add older lines only if you can really patch them.
Add a supported-versions table to SECURITY.md that says when each line stops getting security fixes.
When you fix a vulnerability, release it for every supported line at once and list each patched version in the advisory.
Release small and often so a fix can ship quickly. Mockoon moved to monthly or bi-monthly releases partly so security updates reach users sooner.
Announce end-of-life dates ahead of time in release notes, and update the table when a new major comes out.

items.label: Reproducible builds
items.title: Make builds reproducible
items.short: Make builds reproducible so anyone can rebuild a release and get identical bytes.
items.why: If a release can be rebuilt bit for bit from the tagged source, a tampered artifact or a compromised build machine shows up as a mismatch anyone can check. Expect real work: virtualenv found its rebuilds didn't match because the SBOM in its wheel recorded build-machine details, and had to remove them.
steps: Build the same tag twice, on different machines or days, and compare checksums. Use diffoscope to see what differs.
Fix timestamps: export SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH from the last commit time, which many build tools honor. Maven uses project.build.outputTimestamp; GoReleaser uses mod_timestamp with -trimpath.
Remove build paths, hostnames, usernames and random IDs from outputs, including generated metadata such as SBOMs.
Pin the toolchain and build dependencies by version and hash. virtualenv pinned its build backend and SBOM tools.
Add a CI job that rebuilds the latest release and fails on a mismatch, and publish checksums with every release.

items.label: Validate, sanitize and sandbox untrusted input (allow-lists, CSP)
items.title: Validate and sandbox untrusted input
items.short: Map where untrusted data enters; validate it, cap its size and isolate risky parsing.
items.why: Parsers, decoders and command builders are where attackers get in. aiohttp had to fix a decompression bomb and resource limits that only applied after attacker-controlled buffering, and virtualenv published 21 advisories in five weeks, several of them cases where a path or prompt became a shell command.
steps: List every entry point: uploads, network input, CLI arguments, environment, config files and fetched content. For Readest, book ingestion was the clearest attack surface.
Validate against what's allowed (type, length, format, character set) rather than blocking known-bad input, and do it where the data is used.
Cap size, nesting and time before you buffer or decompress, and process large input in bounded chunks. aiohttp now holds 256 KiB instead of 32 MiB.
Never build shell commands, SQL or HTML by joining strings. Use argument lists, parameterized queries and context-aware escaping.
Allow-list what input can trigger. cdxgen closed whole classes of bugs with allow-lists for external commands and remote hosts.
Parse or render risky formats with as little privilege as you can: a strict Content Security Policy for HTML (Readest) or a separate sandboxed process.

snippets.label: Python: cap decompressed size and keep the shell out of it
snippets.code:
import subprocess
import zlib

MAX_OUTPUT = 10 * 1024 * 1024  # refuse anything that inflates past 10 MiB


def inflate(data: bytes) -> bytes:
    d = zlib.decompressobj()
    out = d.decompress(data, MAX_OUTPUT)
    if d.unconsumed_tail:
        raise ValueError("decompressed data too large")
    return out


def run_tool(path: str) -> str:
    # Argument list, no shell: a file named "x; rm -rf ~" stays one argument.
    # "--" (if the tool supports it) stops a name like "-rf" being read as an option.
    result = subprocess.run(["tool", "--", path], check=True, capture_output=True, text=True)
    return result.stdout

pitfalls: Validating only in the browser or client. Check again where the data is used.
Editing data after escaping it. One of virtualenv's bugs was a later replacement that changed an already-quoted value.
Size limits that are checked after the whole input is already in memory.

Set each default to the safe value: listen on localhost, verify certificates, require auth, and leave debug and risky features off.
Make the unsafe choice explicit: a clearly named option, a warning while it's on, and docs that say what it exposes.
Mask secrets in UIs by default and keep the safe path consistent, so muscle memory doesn't pick the risky option (Polly's advice).
When you tighten a default, say so in the release notes with a migration path. OpenClaw tightened workspace restrictions and accepted the complaints.
Add tests that assert the defaults, so a refactor can't flip them silently.

items.label: Keep secrets out of logs, output and plaintext (redaction)
items.title: Keep secrets out of logs and output
items.short: Keep tokens and passwords out of logs, error messages, crash reports and AI prompts.
items.why: Logs, CI output and bug reports end up pasted into public issues. GoReleaser 2.14 sends command output through a redactor that replaces secret-looking environment variables with their names, and OpenClaw moved credentials to references so they don't end up in prompts, logs or transcripts.
steps: Find the leak paths: log calls, exception messages, debug and verbose output, config dumps, telemetry and crash reports.
Redact in one place: send subprocess and HTTP client output through a single helper before it's printed, as GoReleaser does (example below).
Pass secrets by reference (an env var name or secret store key) and load them where they're used, not into config objects you print.
In GitHub Actions, mask values you create at runtime with ::add-mask:: before anything prints them.
Strip credentials from URLs (https://user:token@host) and connection strings before logging them.
Add a test that runs your verbose mode with a fake token and fails if the token shows up in the output.

snippets.label: Python: redact secret-looking environment values before logging
snippets.code:
import os
import re

# Env var names that usually hold secrets
SECRET_NAME = re.compile(r"TOKEN|SECRET|PASSWORD|PASSWD|API_?KEY|PRIVATE_KEY", re.IGNORECASE)


def redact(text: str) -> str:
    """Replace values of secret-looking env vars with $NAME, as GoReleaser does."""
    for name, value in os.environ.items():
        if len(value) >= 8 and SECRET_NAME.search(name):
            text = text.replace(value, f"${name}")
    return text

# Use it on anything you print or log, for example:
# log.info(redact(proc.stdout))

pitfalls: Exact-match masking misses encoded forms. A base64- or URL-encoded token still leaks.
set -x in CI shell scripts prints every expanded variable, including tokens GitHub doesn't know to mask.
Error messages that include a full connection string, password and all.

items.label: Use memory-safe languages for risky components
items.title: Use memory-safe languages for risky parts
items.short: Write new parsers and risky parts in a memory-safe language, and harden the C you keep.
items.why: In C and C++, a malformed file or packet can corrupt memory and turn into code execution; OpenSSF notes that many vulnerabilities involve memory safety. Stalwart, written in Rust, says the language's memory-safety guarantees and its community's habits meant many of the program's recommendations were already in place.
steps: Write new code that handles untrusted input (file formats, network protocols, decompression) in Rust, Go or another memory-safe language. This is a long-term change, not a sprint task.
For existing C or C++, replace the riskiest parser first, behind the same API, instead of rewriting everything.
Until then, run tests under AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer in CI and fuzz the C entry points. OSS-Fuzz was already catching crashes in Matplotlib's C extensions.
Build with the compiler hardening flags from OpenSSF's hardening guide for C and C++.
In Rust, keep unsafe rare and reviewed, and add #![forbid(unsafe_code)] to crates that don't need it.
Memory-safe code still panics or hangs on bad input, so fuzz it too.

snippets.label: Test C/C++ under AddressSanitizer and UBSan (gcc or clang)
snippets.code:
export CFLAGS="-O1 -g -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer -fno-sanitize-recover=all"
export CXXFLAGS="$CFLAGS"
export LDFLAGS="-fsanitize=address,undefined"
# then your usual build and test commands, for example:
make clean && make && make check

pitfalls: Big-bang rewrites stall. Replace one module at a time and keep the old tests running against it.

items.title: Write fuzz targets for your parsers
items.short: Write fuzz targets for every parser of untrusted input, and run them in CI.
items.why: A fuzzer throws millions of mutated inputs at one function and reports the crashes, hangs and runaway memory that example-based tests miss. Sniffnet's maintainer calls targeted testing and fuzzing the most effective way to find flaws specific to your code.
steps: Pick entry points that take bytes or text from outside: file and protocol parsers, decoders, decompressors, query or template parsers. Start with the one that has had bugs.
Write one small target per entry point with your language's standard fuzzer (below). Expect an hour or two for the first; shadcn/ui used Copilot to set theirs up.
Catch only the errors your API documents and let everything else crash. Assert properties too, such as decode(encode(x)) == x or virtualenv's "no extra command runs".
Seed each target with a few real inputs and keep every crasher as a regression test: Go saves them in testdata/fuzz/, and Jazzer replays its inputs in normal test runs.
Build and briefly run every target in CI so it doesn't rot. ONNX added a CI smoke test for its harnesses, and mimetype caches its corpus between runs.
Fuzz on more than one platform if you do size or integer math. mimetype added 32-bit runs to catch panics like its issue #829.

# Run:   python fuzz/fuzz_parse.py -max_total_time=60
import sys

import atheris

with atheris.instrument_imports():

@atheris.instrument_func
def test_one_input(data: bytes) -> None:

    text = fdp.ConsumeUnicodeNoSurrogates(4096)
    try:

    except mylib.ParseError:

    atheris.Fuzz()

items.title: Fuzz continuously (OSS-Fuzz, ClusterFuzzLite)
items.short: Fuzz around the clock: join OSS-Fuzz if you qualify, otherwise run ClusterFuzzLite.
items.why: A short CI run catches regressions, but deep bugs take hours or days of fuzzing to reach. aiohttp's parsers have been fuzzed continuously by OSS-Fuzz since 2022, and quic-go turned on ClusterFuzzLite batch fuzzing during its sprint.
steps: Write fuzz targets first (see the harness item), then check OSS-Fuzz. It's free and accepts projects with a significant user base or that are critical to global IT infrastructure.
To apply, open a pull request to google/oss-fuzz adding projects/<name>/project.yaml (below). After it's accepted, add a Dockerfile and build.sh following the new project guide.
Once on OSS-Fuzz, add CIFuzz from its docs: by default it fuzzes each PR for 10 minutes and fails only on new crashes. CPython runs it for two OSS-Fuzz projects.
Not eligible, or want it in your own CI? Use ClusterFuzzLite: a .clusterfuzzlite/ folder (project.yaml, Dockerfile, build.sh) plus the PR workflow below. Byte Buddy and Diesel use it.
Add scheduled batch fuzzing, a daily prune job and a corpus storage repo so PR runs start from saved inputs, as quic-go did. Scope that repo's token to it alone.
Give crash reports an owner. CPython created a GitHub team for its fuzzers, and aiohttp plans to move its OSS-Fuzz files into its own repo.

name: ClusterFuzzLite PR fuzzing
on:
  pull_request:
permissions: read-all

        uses: google/clusterfuzzlite/actions/build_fuzzers@884713a6c30a92e5e8544c39945cd7cb630abcd1 # v1

items.short: Threat-model AI features: trace where untrusted text reaches a model that can act.
items.why: Prompt injection can ride on any text a model reads, so an issue body, document or web page can steer a model that has tools. CocoIndex mapped poisoned embeddings and prompt injection through source data, and DocsGPT threat-modeled its code-execution feature before shipping it, so the mitigations were designed in rather than bolted on.
steps: Draw the flow: everything the model reads (prompts, documents, web pages, issues, tool output) and everything it can do (tools, code, writes, network, spending).
Mark each input trusted or not. Nasiko treats issue bodies, PR descriptions, READMEs and code comments as untrusted agent input.
Walk through STRIDE plus AI-specific threats: prompt injection, poisoned data or embeddings, excessive tool permissions, secret leakage, runaway loops and cost.
For each risky path, add a control the model can't talk its way past: schemas, least-privilege tools, approvals, budgets, stop conditions and audit logs (DataJourney's list).
Publish it with what's in and out of scope. aiohttp and DocsGPT note that AI tools and researchers can use a public threat model to rule out non-issues.
Update it when you add a tool, model or data source, and after each advisory, as aiohttp does.
pitfalls: Treating the system prompt as a security boundary. Injected text can override it.
Modeling only the chat box. Retrieved documents, files and tool output are inputs too.
Relying on the model to refuse instead of limiting what its tools can do.

Split reads from writes, and expose only the writes the agent needs through an explicit allowlist.

Require human approval before consequential actions such as merging, publishing or deleting. CAMEL-AI made this a core feature.
Review and pin MCP servers like any dependency, and pass secrets by reference so they stay out of prompts and transcripts (OpenClaw).
Log tool calls so you can see afterwards what an agent did.

items.label: Sandbox code execution and agents; restrict egress
items.title: Sandbox code execution and agents
items.short: Run model-written code and agents in a sandbox with no secrets and limited network.
items.why: If an agent or code-interpreter feature runs code an attacker can influence, the sandbox is all that stands between them and your secrets and network. DocsGPT's sandbox scrubs API keys, tokens and the database URL, blocks internal IP ranges and the cloud metadata endpoint, and ships off by default.
steps: Ship code execution off by default and make turning it on an explicit admin decision, as DocsGPT does.
Run each job in a fresh container or VM as a non-root user, with a read-only filesystem and limits on CPU, memory, processes and wall-clock time.
Start it with an empty environment: no API keys, tokens or database URLs.
Deny network access by default. If code needs the internet, block private ranges and the cloud metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254) so it can't reach internal services.
For coding agents, turn on the agent's own sandbox and keep separate agents and credentials per trust boundary (OpenClaw's advice).
Test the walls: try to read env vars, reach the metadata endpoint and write outside the work directory, and keep those checks in CI.

# No network, read-only root, unprivileged user, capped resources, nothing secret in its env.
# Enforce a wall-clock limit from the caller as well.
docker run --rm --network none --read-only \
  --user 65534:65534 --cap-drop ALL --security-opt no-new-privileges \
  --memory 512m --cpus 1 --pids-limit 128 \
  --tmpfs /tmp:rw,noexec,nosuid,size=64m \
  -v "$PWD/job:/work:ro" \
  your-sandbox-image python /work/script.py

kind: NetworkPolicy

  name: sandbox-egress
spec:

    matchLabels:

  policyTypes:
    - Egress
  egress:

        - protocol: TCP

items.title: Set rules for AI-generated PRs and reports
items.short: Write down how you handle AI-assisted PRs and reports, and ask for evidence: tests for a PR, a proof of concept for a report.
items.why: AI makes plausible-looking PRs and vulnerability reports cheap to produce and costly to review. OpenClaw received 1,309 advisories in under four months and closed 746 as invalid, including 95 of the 109 rated critical, and curl ended its bug bounty in January 2026 after a flood of reports that sounded technical but contained nothing exploitable.
steps: Decide your stance and put it in CONTRIBUTING.md: allowed with disclosure (Sniffnet), case by case (Cobra: "Let AI handle the volume. Stay responsible for the judgment."), or not accepted (Gleam).
Require contributors to understand every line they submit and to say which AI tools they used. That is the first of Sniffnet's 10 contributing rules.
Add a section to SECURITY.md. Like actix-web, accept AI-assisted reports but reject fully AI-generated ones that lack project-specific details and a credible reproduction or impact.
Make it enforceable: a PR template that asks how the change was tested, and a custom private-report form that requires a proof of concept (snippets below).
Publish a trust model or threat model to check reports against. OpenClaw's SECURITY.md gives maintainers "something concrete to point at when closing bad reports."
On PRs, look for evidence: tests, screenshots, agent transcripts and the contributor's own reasoning, the signals OpenClaw now looks for.

Ask AI to explain alerts and suggest mitigations. Keycloak used Copilot to understand CodeQL reports.
Now and then, run an AI-assisted audit guided by your threat model. aiohttp ran GitHub Security Lab's taskflow agent across all aio-libs repositories.
Reproduce every AI finding before you file or fix it. Maintainers stay responsible for what ships (Readest).
Keep CodeQL, dependency scanning and tests as the merge gate. Nasiko treats AI as another set of eyes, not the gate.
Put limits on autonomous agents: cap their open PRs, dedupe their work, and make their commits show they came from a bot.

## Security rules for contributors

1. Never report a vulnerability in a public issue or PR. Use the private form linked in SECURITY.md.
2. Never commit secrets, tokens or real credentials, not even in tests or fixtures. If push protection blocks you, remove the secret; don't bypass.
3. Changes under `.github/` (workflows, CODEOWNERS) need a maintainer's review. Don't add `pull_request_target` triggers or new secrets.
4. Open an issue before adding a dependency, and say why it's needed.
5. Treat input from users, files and the network as untrusted, and validate it where it enters.
6. Every security fix needs a regression test.
7. AI-assisted code is welcome if you understand every line and say which tool you used.

items.title: Share what you learned
items.short: Write up what you changed and why, and publish templates others can copy.
items.why: Security knowledge scales one-to-many: every published lesson saves the next maintainer from learning it the hard way. Fastify wrote up the three changes "you can copy into your own organization today", GoReleaser published an example-secure repository, and Node.js's post on hardening GitHub Actions was "shared widely within the ecosystem".
steps: Write a short post: what you changed, why, what it cost, and what you'd do first next time. Include the config others can copy.
Publish reusable pieces such as your SECURITY.md, incident plan, threat model or workflows; scikit-learn shared a list of the public training material from its cohort.
Talk to your ecosystem: evcc joined a Fund panel and a podcast, virtualenv gave a PyBeach talk, and Typelevel planned a Scala Days talk.
Help a neighbor: kgateway applied its lessons to agentgateway, and nvm planned to share its playbook with Express.
When you find a flaw in someone else's project, report it privately and write it up after the fix, as ImageMagick's maintainer did for a popular editor extension.
pitfalls: Publishing details of issues that aren't fixed yet, or the contacts and procedures in your internal incident plan. As Nasiko puts it, the plan may stay internal; the lessons don't have to.

items.label: Apply for free support programs (funding, audits, AI tools)
items.title: Apply for free support programs
items.short: Free money, audits and AI tools exist for maintainers. Apply to the ones your project fits.
items.why: Several programs give open source maintainers security help at no cost: funding with security training, free audits and hardening, and free AI coding tools. This guide itself is built from what the projects in one of them, GitHub's Secure Open Source Fund, changed. Each program picks its own projects, so the site doesn't check whether you're in any of them: this is a list to apply from.
steps: GitHub Secure Open Source Fund: $10,000 per project, paid to the maintainers over a year, and a 3-week security program with GitHub Security Lab (about 15 hours), then check-ins at 6 and 12 months. It's for up to 2 maintainers of an open source project with a clear license, clear governance and real adoption. Applications are rolling and count for every session.

Claude for Open Source (Anthropic): 6 months of Claude Ultra for maintainers. Any one route qualifies, such as 500 or more dependent repos, 100 or more dependent packages, 200,000 or more monthly downloads, being a listed maintainer of a recognized foundation or language project, or a repo with an OpenSSF criticality score of 0.4 or more. Anthropic also says to apply anyway if the ecosystem quietly depends on your work. It's separate from Anthropic's OSS Scanner, which scans the project itself (its own check in this guide).
Codex for Open Source (OpenAI): API credits, ChatGPT Pro with Codex and, for some, access to Codex Security, for maintainers of widely used projects. Anyone can nominate a maintainer.

Sovereign Tech Resilience (Germany's Sovereign Tech Agency): free work by partner firms for open source that critical digital infrastructure depends on: security audits, supply chain hardening (reproducible builds, signed releases), memory-safety transitions, post-quantum readiness, Cyber Resilience Act compliance and technical debt. Apply through its portal; applications are reviewed as they come in. Its bug and fix bounties were paused in September 2026 while it works through a backlog.
In each application, say why your project matters: who depends on it, where untrusted input enters it, how many downloads it has. Most of these decide case by case, and one clear sentence helps.
pitfalls: Some programs ask for your time as well: the Fund's sessions are mandatory. Read the terms before you apply.
Free AI tools don't change who signs off on a fix. Keep a human review on security changes, whatever wrote them.
These programs change often. Check each program's page for its current criteria and dates; this list was checked in November 2026.
